gaps.note: A commercial break edit interrupts the negotiation just after the founders state a $6 million valuation.

stage_a.note: Both founders maintain strong, enthusiastic smiles and positive vocal delivery throughout the prepared presentation.
The founders show sustained engaged excitement about their product's features and its cost-saving benefits.
The founders are highly approachable and friendly, introducing themselves warmly to the panel.

venture.description: A subscription service and app that prints 100 smartphone photos into a bound, perforated book and mails it to customers monthly.
venture.note: They ask for $150k for 20% of their company.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian introduces himself and Julie, stating their ask of 150k for 20 percent of Groovebook.

turns.speaker: F2
turns.summary: Julie highlights the problem of people taking billions of smartphone photos but doing nothing with them.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian explains the Groovebook app, where users select 100 photos for a monthly bound book.

turns.speaker: F2
turns.summary: Julie describes the book's features, including date stamps, perforated edges for easy removal, and size.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Lori points to a photo in the display and asks if it is Daymond.

turns.speaker: F2
turns.summary: Julie confirms the photo is of Daymond.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Daymond confirms it is a picture of him.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Robert jokes about Daymond having hair in the old photo.

turns.speaker: F2
turns.summary: Julie joins in the joke about Daymond's hair.

turns.speaker: F2
turns.summary: Julie compares Groovebook's cost and convenience favorably against expensive traditional photo books and store printing.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian concludes the pitch and Julie hands out custom Groovebooks to each of the sharks.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Robert reacts positively upon receiving his custom Groovebook.

turns.speaker: F2
turns.summary: Julie thanks the sharks as she finishes handing out the books.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Kevin asks Brian what the retail price of the book is for a customer.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian states the price is 2.99 a month, which includes shipping and handling.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Lori praises the price and asks what it costs them to manufacture the book.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian answers that it costs 2.30 to make each book.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Lori notes that their profit margin per book is very small.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian confirms they make a 70 cent profit margin on each book.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Daymond asks if they have any current sales.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian reports they have acquired 18,000 paid subscribers over the last eight months.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Robert asks them to calculate their total monthly profit based on those numbers.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian explains they are not profitable yet and need 30,000 customers to reach break-even.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Lori asks why they are losing money, prompting about their overhead costs.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian answers that their monthly overhead is 21,000 dollars.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Lori asks who is actually manufacturing the photo books.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian explains that they manufacture the books themselves in their own commercial print shop.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Daymond challenges their pricing strategy, asking why they haven't tried charging more.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian responds that they want the price low so everyone in America can afford it.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Mark challenges Brian's logic, noting that a failed business serves no one.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Daymond agrees with Mark, reiterating that low prices won't help if they go bankrupt.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Mark asks how much of their own money they have invested in Groovebook.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian states he has invested 400,000 dollars.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Robert asks if their manufacturing costs would be higher if they had to use an outside printer.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian says no, citing his proprietary software and specialized equipment.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Robert clarifies, asking if the cost would indeed be higher elsewhere.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian confirms that the cost would be higher with an outside printer.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Robert points out the risk that Groovebook depends entirely on the survival of Brian's other printing business.

turns.speaker: F2
turns.summary: Julie deflects the challenge by explaining how Brian invented the flexible groove to solve shipping damage.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian explains that the patent-pending flexible groove allows them to mail the book for just 82 cents.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Mark acknowledges that the cheap shipping method is the core value proposition.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Robert asks how much shipping would cost without the flexible binding.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian answers that shipping would increase by three to four dollars.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Kevin asks to confirm that the groove is protectable and patent-pending.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian confirms it is patent-pending and calls it their most valuable asset.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Kevin asks if they would be open to raising their subscription price by one dollar.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian affirms that they would be open to raising the price.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Mark suggests pivoting to a B2B service model, licensing the technology to companies like Shutterfly.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian agrees, noting the massive price difference between their book and competitors' average books.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Mark emphasizes focusing on licensing the unique groove technology as an add-on service rather than competing on retail price.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian agrees, highlighting their unique shipping cost advantage.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Mark explains how licensing the service would turn Brian into a passive money collector.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian briefly agrees with Mark's vision.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Robert agrees with Mark's licensing idea and reiterates the risk of relying on the printing business.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Mark offers 150k for 100 percent of the licensing rights, letting them keep the subscription business.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Robert exits, stating the risk of the printing business failing is too high for him.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Daymond agrees with Robert about the structural risk and also exits.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Kevin asks if they would be willing to sell the entire company.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian says they would consider selling for the right price.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Kevin reminds them of their implied valuation and asks again if they would sell.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Kevin offers 750k to buy 100 percent of the entire business.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian states they want to retain some upside in the business.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Mark clarifies his offer, emphasizing they keep their subscription business while he builds the licensing side.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Kevin reiterates his offer to buy the whole company at their stated valuation.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian counters Kevin's offer, stating they believe the company is now worth 6 million dollars.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Lori expresses shock at Brian's high counter-valuation.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Lori recaps the two standing offers from Mark and Kevin.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Daymond points out that Brian originally valued the company at 750k.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian justifies the higher valuation by saying they want to retain upside.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Kevin argues that they cannot arbitrarily multiply their valuation by six just to sell control.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian asks Kevin directly if he accepts or rejects the 6 million dollar valuation.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Kevin firmly rejects the 6 million dollar valuation.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian asks Kevin for middle ground and questions if Kevin wants them to have equity.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Kevin asks Brian how much equity they want to retain.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian states he wants to retain at least 50 percent of the company.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian tells Mark he wants equity in the licensing business since he will be manufacturing for it.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Mark asks Brian what he thinks 50 percent of the company is currently worth.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian states that 50 percent of Groovebook is worth 375,000 dollars.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Robert clarifies if Brian would sell half the company for 375k.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian confirms he would sell 50 percent for 375,000 dollars.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian asks Mark if he is interested in the 375k for 50 percent deal.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Mark declines Brian's proposed 50 percent deal.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Lori offers 375k for 50 percent of the whole business, inviting Robert to join her.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Robert agrees to join Lori's offer.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Lori clarifies their offer is for the entire business, prohibiting outside licensing.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Mark asks Brian if he will accept Lori and Robert's offer.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian emphatically rejects Lori and Robert's offer.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Kevin announces he is joining Mark, revising the licensing offer to take 80 percent instead of 100.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Mark explains their strategy to target one-off photo printing customers through licensing.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Lori argues that under her deal, they would also capture the one-off market.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Daymond uses a movie analogy to warn Brian about the risks of Mark and Kevin's licensing deal.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Mark counters Daymond's warning, explaining how the licensing integration would work.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Lori summarizes the two competing offers on the table for Brian to choose between.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian defends their success in growing the subscription business independently.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian states his preference for Mark and Kevin's deal because they keep the subscription business.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Daymond asks Brian directly if he is accepting Mark and Kevin's offer.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian accepts Mark and Kevin's revised offer.

decisions.terms: $150,000 for 100% of the rights to sell Groovebook as a service
decisions.note: Mark offers 150k for 100 percent of the licensing rights, letting them keep the subscription business.
Reliance on your commercial printing business is too risky.
Agrees with Robert, if the printing business fails this fails.
Kevin offers to buy the whole company at their stated valuation.
Lori offers 375k for 50 percent of the whole business, inviting Robert to join her.

decisions.terms: Happy to go in with it
decisions.note: Robert re-enters and agrees to join Lori's offer.
Kevin joins Mark and revises the offer to take 80 percent instead of 100.
Accepts Mark and Kevin's revised offer for the licensing business.

record.notes: Robert exits at 6:25 but re-enters at 10:25 to join Lori's offer. The negotiation has a significant edit around 8:11 right after Brian counters with a $6 million valuation.
